lessons.title: Getting animals ready in the lairage
lessons.html:
Getting animals ready in the lairage

Before slaughter, animals rest in the pens (the lairage). Good preparation gives clean, safe meat and a calm animal at the stunning box.

Rest

Animals get tired and stressed on the truck. A rest in the pens with water lets them calm down. Your abattoir has rules on how long animals rest and how long feed is held back before slaughter. Follow those rules and the instructions of your supervisor.

Water, but no feed

  • Animals always get clean drinking water in the pens.
  • Feed is usually held back for a time before slaughter. An empty stomach and gut are less likely to burst during dressing. A burst gut spills dung onto the meat.

Clean animals

  • Dirty animals bring mud and dung into the slaughter hall. This dirt carries germs that can make people sick.
  • Some abattoirs wash cattle or pigs with a water spray before slaughter. Use the spray gently and never point it at the face.
  • Report very dirty animals to your supervisor. The meat inspector may decide how they must be handled.
  • Sheep must be dry before slaughter. Wet wool makes it hard to keep the carcass clean.

Identify the animals

Each animal or group must be identified so the carcass can be traced back to the owner. Keep pen cards and lot numbers correct. Never mix animals from different owners without recording it. If an animal loses its ear tag or mark, tell your supervisor.

Check before moving

Only animals passed by the meat inspector at the ante mortem inspection may go to slaughter. Animals that are held back must stay in their pen until the inspector says what to do.

lessons.title: Moving animals to the stunning box
lessons.html:
Moving animals to the stunning box

The last part of preparation is moving animals from the pens through the race to the stunning box. This must be done quietly and safely.

Steps

  1. Check the race and the box. Remove anything that scares animals: shadows, hanging chains, water puddles, loose plastic.
  2. Move a small group from the pen. Animals follow each other.
  3. Work behind the shoulder of the animal to make it walk forward. Use a flag or paddle.
  4. Keep a steady flow. Do not push more animals into the race than the stunner can handle. Animals should not wait for a long time in the race.
  5. Close gates behind the animals so they cannot turn back.
  6. One animal at a time goes into the stunning box.

Never

  • Never hit, kick or shout at animals.
  • Never twist tails or poke eyes.
  • Never leave an animal in the stunning box for a long time. If there is a problem at the stunner, stop sending animals and tell your supervisor.

Cruelty to animals is a crime under the Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962.

Your safety

  • Wear safety boots and your protective clothing.
  • Stay outside the race when possible. Use the catwalk.
  • Keep your hands out of gates and between moving animals and steel bars.
  • Know where the emergency stop button is.

Hygiene

  • Clean the pens and race at the end of the day.
  • Wash your boots in the boot wash when moving from the pens to the clean area.

Key points

  • Animals rest with water before slaughter. Feed is held back as your abattoir rules say.
  • Clean, dry animals give cleaner meat.
  • Keep pen cards and lot numbers correct so carcasses can be traced.
  • Only animals passed by the meat inspector may go to slaughter.
  • Move small groups quietly and keep a steady flow to the stunner.

quiz.question: Why is feed held back before slaughter?

options.text: So the gut is less likely to burst and spill dung on the meat
